title: Repairing the world
hookLine: Luria's cosmic tikkun later became a word for social justice

cards: Near the end of the service in the Jewish prayer book stands a prayer called Aleinu.
Toward its close is a hope, and in Hebrew it reads l'taken olam b'malchut Shaddai: to set the world right under the kingdom of the Almighty.
Today, that short phrase, tikkun olam, turns up on synagogue banners, on school volunteer days, on the side of a food drive.
How did a line from a prayer, and a teaching about broken vessels, end up on a sign by the canned goods? It has quite a road behind it.

teach.b: Repairing the world. Tikkun olam. Follow the phrase four steps down its road.
First, the law. In the Mishnah, the rabbis make certain rulings, they say, for the sake of tikkun ha'olam. Rules about how a divorce document is written, so no one is trapped by a careless name.

A rule that captives are not ransomed for more than they're worth; one reason later readers give is that kidnapping shouldn't become a business. Here, repairing the world means keeping society fair and in working order.
In the Aleinu, the phrase lifts its eyes. It becomes a hope for the whole world, set right under God's kingship. Not a rule anymore, a horizon.
Third, Luria. In his teaching, tikkun becomes cosmic. The vessels broke; the sparks fell.
Every commandment and every kind act gathers a spark and mends a piece of what shattered. Repair isn't only for society now. It's for creation itself, and every person has a share in it.
In more recent times, tikkun olam has become a common name for work for justice: feeding the hungry, caring for the earth, standing up for people pushed aside. Some teachers welcome that wide use.
Others ask that it keep its roots in the commandments and in prayer. Both are Jewish voices, and both are part of its story.
Read this way, what ties the four together is the sense that the world is not finished, and that people's hands belong in the finishing. A rule, a prayer, a spark, a sandwich handed across a table.

how: Tikkun olam is spoken of in Jewish schools, synagogues and community groups as a reason for charity and justice work, while the phrase also stays in the Aleinu prayer said in services.

o: the yearly cleaning of the home before Passover
a fund synagogues keep for fixing their buildings
setting the world right, from law and prayer to justice

p: a hope for the world set right

s: tikkun olam is a modern invention
the phrase is already in the Mishnah's rulings and in the Aleinu prayer.
the Mishnah makes some rulings for the sake of repairing the world
rules about divorce documents and ransoming captives, to keep society fair.
for Luria, tikkun meant only social action
for Luria, it was cosmic: gathering the sparks and mending what shattered.

games.q: you see tikkun olam printed on a food-drive sign. where, by today's story, has that phrase been before?
o: nowhere: it's a slogan made up for signs.
in the Mishnah, the Aleinu, and Luria's teaching.
games.why: the phrase moves through the Mishnah's rulings, the Aleinu prayer and Luria's cosmic repair before it reaches justice work today.

practice: Bring to mind one small thing you did recently: holding a door, paying someone on time, calling a parent.
Widen the view, who it touched and who they go on to touch, like rings on water, until it looks like one stitch in something much larger. Then come back to the one act, and rest there.

wordCard.voice: Repairing the world. Tikkun olam: a phrase that runs from the Mishnah's fair rulings, through the Aleinu and Luria's mending of creation, to work for justice today. Today's words.

orig.note: Hebrew: the repair, or setting right, of the world.
